title: Physiology III: Renal, Body Fluids and Gastrointestinal (PIO 212/216)
description: Glomerular filtration, tubular function, urine concentration and acid–base balance, plus gastrointestinal motility, secretion, digestion and absorption.

topics.title: Glomerular Filtration and Renal Blood Flow
topics.summary: The nephron, filtration forces, GFR, clearance and autoregulation.

notes.b: The kidneys receive about 20–25% of cardiac output (≈ 1.1–1.25 L/min). Each kidney has about one million nephrons. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 125 mL/min (180 L/day). Net filtration pressure = glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure − (Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure + plasma oncotic pressure). The filtration barrier (fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms) restricts proteins by size and negative charge, so albumin is normally not filtered in significant amounts. Renal blood flow and GFR are autoregulated between MAP of about 80–180 mmHg by the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback (macula densa).

Clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute: C = (U × V) / P. Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR (the gold standard); creatinine clearance is used clinically (slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted). PAH clearance measures effective renal plasma flow (~625 mL/min). Filtration fraction = GFR/RPF ≈ 20%. Glucose is fully reabsorbed until the renal threshold (plasma ~180–200 mg/dL) is exceeded, as in uncontrolled diabetes (glycosuria).

topics.title: Tubular Function, Urine Concentration and Diuretics
topics.summary: Reabsorption and secretion along the nephron, countercurrent mechanism, ADH and aldosterone.

notes.b: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs about 65–70% of filtered Na+ and water, nearly all glucose and amino acids, and most bicarbonate. The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle reabsorbs Na+, K+ and 2 Cl− via the NKCC2 co-transporter (blocked by loop diuretics like furosemide) and is impermeable to water, diluting the tubular fluid. The distal convoluted tubule reabsorbs NaCl via the Na–Cl co-transporter (blocked by thiazides). The collecting duct principal cells reabsorb Na+ and secrete K+ under aldosterone (ENaC channels, blocked by amiloride; aldosterone blocked by spironolactone).
k: PCT: ~65% of Na+ and water, all glucose
Thiazides block NCC in the DCT

notes.b: The countercurrent multiplier of the loop of Henle and urea recycling create a hyperosmotic medullary interstitium (up to ~1,200 mOsm/kg); the vasa recta act as countercurrent exchangers preserving it. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary, released when plasma osmolality rises or blood volume falls, inserts aquaporin-2 channels in collecting duct cells, allowing water reabsorption and concentrated urine. Lack of ADH or renal unresponsiveness causes diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine). Alcohol inhibits ADH release.

topics.title: Acid–Base Balance
topics.summary: Buffers, renal and respiratory compensation, and interpreting acid–base disorders.

notes.b: Normal arterial pH is 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mmHg and HCO3− 22–26 mmol/L. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for blood is pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3−]/(0.03 × PCO2)). Buffers act instantly; the lungs adjust CO2 within minutes; the kidneys adjust HCO3− and excrete H+ (as titratable acid and ammonium) over hours to days. The anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally about 8–12 mmol/L; a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis occurs in diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure and poisoning (methanol, salicylates).
k: Raised AG: DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure

notes.b: Respiratory acidosis (↑PCO2) — hypoventilation, e.g. COPD, opioid overdose; compensation: ↑HCO3−. Respiratory alkalosis (↓PCO2) — hyperventilation, e.g. anxiety, high altitude; compensation: ↓HCO3−. Metabolic acidosis (↓HCO3−) — DKA, diarrhoea (normal anion gap), renal failure; compensation: hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing). Metabolic alkalosis (↑HCO3−) — vomiting (loss of HCl), diuretics; compensation: hypoventilation.
k: Vomiting → metabolic alkalosis; diarrhoea → metabolic acidosis

topics.title: Gastrointestinal Motility and Secretions
topics.summary: Swallowing, gastric emptying, gastric acid secretion, pancreatic juice and bile.

notes.b: Swallowing has oral (voluntary), pharyngeal and oesophageal (reflex) phases; the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let food into the stomach (failure of relaxation = achalasia). The enteric nervous system (myenteric/Auerbach's plexus controls motility; submucosal/Meissner's plexus controls secretion) is modulated by autonomic nerves: parasympathetic stimulates, sympathetic inhibits. Peristalsis propels contents; segmentation mixes them. Gastric emptying is slowed by fat and acid in the duodenum (via CCK and secretin). The migrating motor complex sweeps the gut between meals (motilin).
k: Fat in duodenum slows gastric emptying

notes.b: Gastric parietal cells secrete HCl (via the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump, blocked by omeprazole) and intrinsic factor (needed for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum); chief cells secrete pepsinogen; G cells in the antrum secrete gastrin. Acid secretion is stimulated by acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine (H2 receptors, blocked by ranitidine/cimetidine) in cephalic, gastric and intestinal phases. Secretin (from duodenal S cells, released by acid) stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice; cholecystokinin (I cells, released by fat and protein) stimulates pancreatic enzymes and gallbladder contraction. Bile salts emulsify fats and are recycled via the enterohepatic circulation.
k: Secretin → bicarbonate; CCK → enzymes + gallbladder contraction

topics.title: Digestion and Absorption
topics.summary: Digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, water and electrolytes.

notes.b: Starch digestion begins with salivary α-amylase and continues with pancreatic amylase to maltose and oligosaccharides; brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase) produce monosaccharides. Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes by SGLT1 (with Na+); fructose by GLUT5; all leave via GLUT2. Lactase deficiency causes lactose intolerance (bloating, diarrhoea). Protein digestion starts with pepsin in the stomach and continues with pancreatic trypsin (activated from trypsinogen by enterokinase/enteropeptidase), chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidases; amino acids, di- and tripeptides are absorbed.

Fats are emulsified by bile salts and digested by pancreatic lipase (with colipase) to monoglycerides and fatty acids, which form micelles for absorption; inside enterocytes they are re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons, which enter lacteals (lymph). Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K need this pathway, so fat malabsorption causes their deficiency. About 9 L of fluid enters the gut daily; most is absorbed in the small intestine and about 1.5 L enters the colon. Cholera toxin raises cAMP, causing massive Cl− and water secretion; oral rehydration solution exploits intact Na+–glucose co-transport.
k: Fat malabsorption → deficiency of A, D, E, K
